title: Protein Turnover and Amino Acid Catabolism: Tag, Recognize, Destroy, Recycle

generated.pipeline: extract → Opus draft → Sonnet accuracy gate → Sonnet fixes

cards.front: The adult human body turns over roughly {{c1::250 grams}} of protein a day.
cards.back: Torn down and rebuilt, even in what looks like a stable adult.
cards.quote: Your body turns over roughly 250 grams of protein a day, tearing down and rebuilding what looks like a stable adult.

cards.front: Ubiquitin's C-terminal Gly-Gly attaches to a lysine on the target protein through an {{c1::isopeptide}} bond.
cards.back: An amide bond to a side-chain amine, not to the backbone.
cards.quote: Its C-terminal Gly-Gly forms an isopeptide bond (an amide bond to a side-chain amine, not to the backbone) with a lysine on the doomed protein.

cards.front: In the ubiquitin cascade, what do E1, E2 and E3 each do?
cards.back: E1 activates ubiquitin, spending ATP to form a thioester to its own cysteine. E2 carries the activated ubiquitin. E3, the ligase, chooses the target and gets the ubiquitin onto it.
cards.quote: E3, the ligase, picks the address: it chooses the target and gets the ubiquitin onto it.

cards.front: Why is the E3 ligase, not E1 or E2, the specificity step of ubiquitin tagging?
cards.back: There are roughly 2 E1s and about 40 E2s but more than 600 E3s. Each E3 picks particular targets, so the choice of which protein dies lives in the E3s.
cards.quote: Count them: roughly 2 E1 enzymes, about 40 E2s and more than 600 E3s.

cards.front: A drug molecule binds a disease-causing protein with one end and an E3 ligase that normally ignores that protein with the other. What happens to the protein, and why is an E3 the right enzyme to recruit?
cards.back: The protein is ubiquitin-tagged and destroyed by the proteasome. E3s are the layer that chooses targets, so bringing an E3 to a new protein redirects destruction to it. This is how PROTAC drugs work.
cards.quote: PROTAC drugs exploit this: they recruit an E3 ligase to a protein it would normally ignore, condemning that protein to the proteasome.

cards.front: Versions of one yeast test protein differ only in the first residue. Methionine, glycine or alanine versions last more than 20 hours; arginine or phenylalanine versions are gone in about two or three minutes. What does this show?
cards.back: The N-end rule: the first residue acts as a degron that sets half-life. One residue changes stability hundreds of fold.
cards.quote: A yeast test protein starting with methionine, glycine or alanine lasted more than 20 hours

cards.front: A chain of four or more {{c1::K48}}-linked ubiquitins is the classic destruction signal.
cards.back: K48 means a link through ubiquitin's own lysine 48.
cards.quote: A chain of four or more K48-linked ubiquitins is the classic destruction signal.

cards.front: A cell's only ubiquitin has lysine 48 replaced by arginine (K48R). Which chain message is lost, and which kind of chain-based signaling can still occur?
cards.back: K48 chains cannot form, so the classic destruction signal is lost. K63 chains can still form, so nonproteolytic signals (DNA repair, trafficking, immune signaling) remain.
cards.why: The chain is a code: the linkage lysine sets the message.
cards.quote: Ubiquitin has lysines of its own, so ubiquitins can be chained; K48 means a link through ubiquitin's lysine 48.

cards.front: What is the structure of the 26S proteasome?
cards.back: One or two 19S caps on a 20S core.
cards.quote: Tagged proteins go to the 26S proteasome, one or two 19S caps on a 20S core.

cards.front: Why does the proteasome rarely degrade untagged bystander proteins?
cards.back: The 20S core's active sites face strictly inward, so bystanders are rarely cut; the 19S cap recognizes the K48 chain, unfolds the protein and threads it in.
cards.quote: The core's active sites face strictly inward, so bystanders are rarely chewed up.

cards.front: Peptide-bond hydrolysis is downhill and trypsin needs no ATP. What does the ubiquitin-proteasome system's ATP buy?
cards.back: Not cutting. ATP at E1 charges ubiquitin so the E3 can mark the target; ATP at the 19S cap unfolds and threads the protein. It buys specificity and processivity.
cards.quote: The ATP buys specificity (the right target) and processivity (once a protein enters, it is cut all the way down to short peptides).

cards.front: A drug blocks ATP use by the 19S cap but leaves the 20S core's active sites intact. What happens to K48-tagged proteins, and why?
cards.back: They accumulate, still tagged. The core cuts without ATP, but the cap needs ATP to unfold and thread proteins in, and the inward-facing sites cannot reach a folded protein.
cards.quote: The caps recognize the K48 chain, unfold the protein and thread it in, using ATP.

cards.front: How does a signal activate NF-κB?
cards.back: Its inhibitor IκB is phosphorylated, tagged with a K48 chain and destroyed. Freed NF-κB enters the nucleus and switches on inflammatory and immune genes. Destroying the inhibitor is the activation.
cards.quote: When a signal arrives, IκB is phosphorylated, tagged with a K48 chain and destroyed, which frees NF-κB to enter the nucleus and switch on inflammatory and immune genes.

cards.front: Cells are treated with a proteasome inhibitor, then given an inflammatory signal. What happens to NF-κB target genes, and why?
cards.back: They stay largely off. IκB can be phosphorylated and tagged but not destroyed, so NF-κB stays trapped outside the nucleus.
cards.quote: NF-κB sits trapped by its inhibitor IκB.

cards.front: In normal oxygen, how is HIF-1α kept low?
cards.back: A prolyl hydroxylase uses O₂ and α-ketoglutarate to hydroxylate HIF-1α. The VHL E3 ligase recognizes the hydroxyproline and sends HIF-1α to the proteasome.
cards.quote: In normal oxygen, a prolyl hydroxylase uses O₂ and α-ketoglutarate to hydroxylate HIF-1α, and the VHL E3 ligase recognizes the hydroxyproline and sends HIF-1α to the proteasome.

cards.front: Oxygen falls in a tissue. What happens to HIF-1α, and why are its target genes switched on?
cards.back: HIF-1α survives. The hydroxylase needs O₂, so without hydroxyproline VHL cannot recognize it. HIF-1α switches on VEGF and glycolytic genes; HIF-2α drives EPO.
cards.quote: Without the hydroxyproline, VHL cannot recognize HIF-1α, and HIF-1α survives.

cards.front: A kidney tumor lacks functional VHL. In normal oxygen, predict HIF-1α levels, and say whether raising oxygen further would lower them.
cards.back: HIF-1α stays high, and more oxygen would not help. Hydroxylation still happens, but no E3 reads the hydroxyproline, so the destruction that normally keeps HIF off never occurs.
cards.quote: Nothing was added to switch the response on; the destruction that kept it off stopped.

cards.front: Why do multiple myeloma plasma cells die first when the proteasome is blocked with bortezomib?
cards.back: They make so much antibody that they depend on clearing misfolded protein. With the proteasome blocked, misfolded protein piles up and kills them.
cards.quote: Multiple myeloma plasma cells churn out so much antibody that they are addicted to clearing misfolded protein.

cards.front: An adult in nitrogen balance breaks down about 250 g of body protein a day and burns about 80 g of amino acids (about what they eat). What fraction of amino acids leaving the pool goes back into protein?
cards.back: Amino acids leaving the pool = 250 g rebuilt + 80 g burned = about 330 g. Fraction reused = 250 / 330 = about 0.76, roughly three-quarters.
cards.quote: about three-quarters of the amino acids leaving the pool go back into protein (250 of about 330 g)
cards.section: From destruction to fuel: most amino acids are reused

cards.front: The body turns over about 250 g of protein a day. Why does most urea not come from that turnover?
cards.back: Turnover is nearly a closed loop: broken-down protein is rebuilt. Urea comes mainly from burning the surplus, after a protein-rich meal or during a fast, plus a small obligatory loss.
cards.quote: Turnover by itself is nearly a closed loop; urea comes mainly from burning the surplus (plus a small obligatory loss)
cards.section: From destruction to fuel: most amino acids are reused

cards.front: At body pH, nearly all ammonia is NH₄⁺; only about {{c1::1 to 3%}} is NH₃.
cards.quote: At body pH nearly all of it is ammonium ion (NH₄⁺); only about 1 to 3% is NH₃

cards.front: For most amino acids, aminotransferases collect the amino group onto α-ketoglutarate, so {{c1::glutamate}} is the nitrogen collection point.
cards.quote: For most amino acids, aminotransferases collect the amino group onto α-ketoglutarate, so glutamate is the collection point.

cards.front: All aminotransferases use the cofactor {{c1::pyridoxal phosphate (PLP, vitamin B6)}}.
cards.quote: They all use pyridoxal phosphate (PLP, vitamin B6).

cards.front: Aspartate carrying a ¹⁵N label is transaminated with α-ketoglutarate. Where is the label afterward, and how much nitrogen has left the amino-acid pool?
cards.back: The ¹⁵N is on glutamate (aspartate becomes oxaloacetate). No nitrogen has left the pool: transamination moves nitrogen, it removes none.
cards.why: Aminotransferases only trade amino groups between amino acids and keto acids, and the reaction is reversible.
cards.quote: Transamination moves nitrogen; it removes none. It is reversible

cards.front: Glutamate dehydrogenase is reversible. Why does it run toward releasing NH₄⁺ in liver mitochondria?
cards.back: The urea cycle drains away the ammonium it makes, pulling the reaction toward release: glutamate + NAD(P)⁺ + H₂O to α-ketoglutarate + NH₄⁺ + NAD(P)H.
cards.quote: in liver the urea cycle drains the ammonium, so it runs toward release.

cards.front: How does the glucose-alanine cycle move nitrogen from muscle to liver?
cards.back: Muscle puts nitrogen onto pyruvate from glycolysis, making alanine. The liver takes the nitrogen off and turns the pyruvate into glucose for muscle and brain.
cards.quote: In the glucose-alanine cycle, muscle puts nitrogen onto pyruvate from glycolysis, making alanine; the liver takes it off and turns the pyruvate into glucose for muscle and brain.

cards.front: Which is the most abundant amino acid in blood, how many nitrogens does it carry, and which enzyme frees one as ammonium?
cards.back: Glutamine; two nitrogens; glutaminase in liver and kidney releases one as ammonium.
cards.quote: Glutamine, the most abundant amino acid in blood, carries two nitrogens; glutaminase in liver and kidney releases one as ammonium.

cards.front: During a fast, ¹⁵N is placed on the amino nitrogen of muscle alanine. Which of urea's two nitrogens can carry the label, and by what routes?
cards.back: Either one. In liver the nitrogen goes to glutamate. Glutamate dehydrogenase can free it as NH₄⁺ for CPS-I (first nitrogen), or glutamate can hand it to oxaloacetate, making aspartate (second nitrogen).
cards.why: Urea takes one nitrogen from free ammonium and one from aspartate, and glutamate feeds both.
cards.quote: The liver now holds waste nitrogen in two forms: free ammonium, and the amino group of aspartate, made when glutamate hands its nitrogen to oxaloacetate.
cards.section: Caging the nitrogen: the urea cycle

cards.front: What enzyme catalyzes the committed, rate-limiting step of the urea cycle, and why does the cycle speed up when amino acids are plentiful?
cards.back: CPS-I, which works only with N-acetylglutamate bound. The liver makes N-acetylglutamate from acetyl-CoA and glutamate faster when amino acids are plentiful, so the cycle speeds up as nitrogen arrives.
cards.quote: CPS-I works only with N-acetylglutamate bound, which the liver makes from acetyl-CoA and glutamate faster when amino acids are plentiful.
cards.section: Caging the nitrogen: the urea cycle

cards.front: A liver cannot make N-acetylglutamate. Predict urea-cycle flux and plasma ammonia.
cards.back: Flux falls and ammonia rises. CPS-I is inactive without N-acetylglutamate, so ammonium is not fixed into carbamoyl phosphate at the committed step.
cards.quote: Carbamoyl phosphate synthetase I (CPS-I) joins ammonium to bicarbonate, spending two ATP, to make carbamoyl phosphate: the committed, rate-limiting step.
cards.section: Caging the nitrogen: the urea cycle

cards.front: Which urea-cycle steps occur in the mitochondrion and which in the cytosol, and which intermediate crosses outward?
cards.back: Steps 1 (CPS-I) and 2 (OTC) are mitochondrial; steps 3 to 5 are cytosolic. Citrulline leaves for the cytosol, and ornithine returns.
cards.quote: Ornithine transcarbamylase (OTC) hands the carbamoyl group to ornithine, making citrulline, which leaves for the cytosol.
cards.section: Caging the nitrogen: the urea cycle

cards.front: In liver slices, a small amount of added ornithine supported far more urea than it could have made itself. What did this show?
cards.back: Ornithine is a regenerated carrier, a catalyst: used at step 2 and returned at step 5. It was the first metabolic cycle described.
cards.quote: Krebs and Henseleit spotted this in liver slices: a little ornithine supported far more urea than it could have made itself.
cards.section: Caging the nitrogen: the urea cycle

cards.front: Where do urea's two nitrogens and its carbon come from?
cards.back: Nitrogen 1 from free ammonium (step 1, CPS-I); nitrogen 2 from aspartate's amino group (step 3); the carbon from bicarbonate (step 1).
cards.quote: Aspartate's amino group is urea's second nitrogen.
cards.section: Caging the nitrogen: the urea cycle

cards.front: Using the gross cost of the urea cycle, how many high-energy phosphate bonds does the liver spend to excrete 10 nitrogen atoms as urea?
cards.back: Each urea carries 2 N, so 10 N = 5 urea. Cost per urea = 2 ATP at step 1 + 2 bonds at step 3 (ATP to AMP + PPᵢ, then PPᵢ split) = 4. Total = 5 x 4 = 20 bonds.
cards.quote: This step spends one ATP but cuts it to AMP and pyrophosphate, and the pyrophosphate is then split, so it costs two high-energy bonds.
cards.section: Caging the nitrogen: the urea cycle

cards.front: Arginase is inhibited in the liver. Predict what happens to arginine, urea output and the urea cycle's turning.
cards.back: Arginine accumulates and urea output falls, because the step that releases urea and regenerates ornithine is blocked.
cards.quote: Arginase adds water to arginine, releasing urea and regenerating ornithine, which returns to the mitochondrion.
cards.section: Caging the nitrogen: the urea cycle

cards.front: Fumarate from the urea cycle becomes malate, then oxaloacetate. Why is this not a source of net new glucose?
cards.back: The oxaloacetate takes an amino group and becomes aspartate again, so the loop only returns the four carbons aspartate brought in. Net glucose carbon comes from glucogenic amino acid skeletons and glycerol.
cards.quote: Oxaloacetate can become glucose, but the loop only returns the carbon aspartate brought in.
cards.section: Caging the nitrogen: the urea cycle

cards.front: Why does urea-cycle failure cause brain edema?
cards.back: Ammonia rises, and astrocytes swell as they trap it in glutamine.
cards.quote: When the cycle fails, ammonia rises and astrocytes swell as they trap it in glutamine, causing brain edema.

cards.front: Why does OTC deficiency raise urinary orotic acid?
cards.back: Carbamoyl phosphate that OTC cannot use spills from the mitochondrion into cytosolic pyrimidine synthesis, whose intermediate orotic acid reaches the urine.
cards.quote: Carbamoyl phosphate that OTC cannot use spills out of the mitochondrion into that pathway, and its intermediate, orotic acid, reaches the urine.

cards.front: An infant has hyperammonemia with markedly high plasma citrulline. Which urea-cycle step is most likely blocked?
cards.back: Argininosuccinate synthetase (step 3), causing citrullinemia. Citrulline is being made, so OTC works, but it cannot be condensed with aspartate and backs up.
cards.quote: Deficiency causes citrullinemia: citrulline backs up because it cannot be condensed with aspartate.

cards.front: Two infants have hyperammonemia and low citrulline. One has high urinary orotic acid; the other does not. Which has CPS-I deficiency and which OTC deficiency?
cards.back: High orotic acid points to OTC deficiency; normal orotic acid points to CPS-I deficiency. With CPS-I blocked, little carbamoyl phosphate is made, so little spills into pyrimidine synthesis.
cards.why: Orotic acid rises when carbamoyl phosphate is made but OTC cannot use it.
cards.quote: The cytosol builds the ring of the pyrimidine bases C, T and U from carbamoyl phosphate and aspartate.

cards.front: Name the seven entry points of amino acid carbon into central metabolism.
cards.back: Pyruvate, α-ketoglutarate, succinyl-CoA, fumarate, oxaloacetate, acetyl-CoA and acetoacetyl-CoA.
cards.quote: All 20 amino acids enter central metabolism at seven doors, some at more than one.

cards.front: Why can carbon entering as acetyl-CoA not become net glucose?
cards.back: Pyruvate dehydrogenase is irreversible, so acetyl-CoA cannot return to pyruvate. Each citric acid cycle turn takes in two carbons and gives off two as CO₂, so no extra oxaloacetate is made.
cards.quote: Pyruvate dehydrogenase is irreversible, so it cannot go back to pyruvate

cards.front: The only two purely ketogenic amino acids are {{c1::leucine and lysine}}.
cards.back: Leucine enters as acetyl-CoA and acetoacetyl-CoA; lysine as acetoacetyl-CoA.
cards.quote: Only two amino acids are purely ketogenic: leucine (acetyl-CoA and acetoacetyl-CoA) and lysine (acetoacetyl-CoA).

cards.front: During a prolonged fast, which of alanine, leucine and lysine can supply net glucose carbon to the liver?
cards.back: Only alanine. It enters at pyruvate, which can become oxaloacetate. Leucine and lysine enter only at acetyl-CoA or acetoacetyl-CoA, which cannot.
cards.quote: The rule: only the first five doors give net glucose, because each can become oxaloacetate, the starting point for glucose.

cards.front: Isoleucine's carbon enters at succinyl-CoA and at acetyl-CoA. Is isoleucine glucogenic, ketogenic, or mixed, and why?
cards.back: Mixed. The succinyl-CoA part can become oxaloacetate and net glucose; the acetyl-CoA part cannot.
cards.quote: Five are mixed: isoleucine, phenylalanine, threonine, tryptophan and tyrosine.

cards.front: How does propionyl-CoA reach succinyl-CoA, and which cofactor does each step use?
cards.back: A biotin enzyme carboxylates propionyl-CoA to methylmalonyl-CoA; methylmalonyl-CoA mutase, a B12 enzyme, rearranges that into succinyl-CoA.
cards.quote: A biotin enzyme carboxylates it to methylmalonyl-CoA, and methylmalonyl-CoA mutase, a B12 enzyme, rearranges that into succinyl-CoA.

cards.front: A patient is deficient in vitamin B12. Which intermediate in the breakdown of valine, isoleucine, methionine and threonine should build up?
cards.back: Methylmalonyl-CoA. B12 is the cofactor for the rearrangement by methylmalonyl-CoA mutase, so that step stalls.
cards.quote: Cofactors fingerprint the step: PLP for amino-group transfer, biotin for carboxylation, B12 for the rearrangement.

cards.front: A patient's liver makes net glucose from alanine and glutamate but not from valine. Which door is affected, and which two cofactor-dependent steps are candidates?
cards.back: The succinyl-CoA door. Valine reaches it via propionyl-CoA, so the cofactor-dependent steps from propionyl-CoA onward are candidates: the biotin carboxylation to methylmalonyl-CoA and the B12 mutase step to succinyl-CoA. Upstream defects are not excluded.
cards.why: Alanine (pyruvate) and glutamate (α-ketoglutarate) use other doors, so gluconeogenesis itself works.
cards.quote: The succinyl-CoA door explains two vitamins. Its four amino acids are broken down to propionyl-CoA.

cards.front: A liver is given ¹³C-labeled leucine, and some label later appears in glucose. Does this show that leucine is glucogenic?
cards.back: No. Over later citric acid cycle turns, acetyl-CoA carbons trade places with oxaloacetate carbons, so a label can reach glucose. But two carbons leave as CO₂ for every two that enter, so no net glucose is made.
cards.quote: So an acetyl-CoA carbon can turn up in glucose as an isotope label, because over later turns it trades places with oxaloacetate carbons.
cards.section: A label is not net glucose

cards.front: Which enzyme is defective in PKU, and how is PKU caught and managed?
cards.back: Phenylalanine hydroxylase. Caught by newborn screening; managed with a low-phenylalanine diet.
cards.quote: PKU (defective phenylalanine hydroxylase) is caught by newborn screening and managed by a low-phenylalanine diet.

cards.front: Which enzyme is defective in maple syrup urine disease (MSUD), and what builds up?
cards.back: Branched-chain keto-acid dehydrogenase. Branched-chain amino acids and their keto acids build up; the excess leucine is neurotoxic.
cards.quote: In MSUD (defective branched-chain keto-acid dehydrogenase), branched-chain amino acids and their keto acids build up

cards.front: The bar-tailed godwit flies 11,000 km nonstop and breaks down some muscle protein on the way. Why does excreting the nitrogen as uric acid rather than urea suit this flight?
cards.back: Uric acid costs almost no water. The bird burns fat for energy and metabolic water and breaks down some muscle protein, probably for glucose, anaplerosis and more water.
cards.quote: The nitrogen leaves as uric acid, which costs almost no water.
cards.section: The whole lesson in one bird

cards.front: During a fast, a muscle protein is destroyed and one of its alanines is burned. Trace where ATP is spent to choose the protein, where the nitrogen ends up, and where the carbon goes.
cards.back: ATP at E1 and the 19S cap tags and unfolds the protein. Alanine's nitrogen travels via the glucose-alanine cycle and glutamate into urea. Its carbon enters at pyruvate and can become net glucose.
cards.why: Choose, then split by atom: E3s pick the target, nitrogen is caged as urea, carbon is kept.
cards.quote: Choose, then split by atom: the E3s pick what dies, the nitrogen is caged, the carbon is kept.
cards.section: The whole lesson in one bird

cards.front: A patient's blood ALT and AST are both high. Why does this suggest liver injury, and why is AST the less specific of the two?
cards.back: These transaminases leak into the blood when liver cells are injured. AST also comes from muscle and heart, so it alone is less specific for liver.
cards.quote: ALT and AST leak into the blood when liver cells are injured, which is why these transaminases sit on standard liver panels.
